This initiative aligned with the Tribe’s vision for responsible energy use, addressing the challenges of high fuel oil prices in a remote community; it could serve as a model for similar efforts in Aniak and other Alaska Native villages pursuing energy self- reliance. 1 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 2.0 Background The Native Village of Aniak (NVA) is a Yup’ik village of about 570 people, located on the Kuskokwim River in Southwest Alaska. In 2017, NVA, supported by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL), obtained energy audits of several Tribal buildings for a project under a previous grant from the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Indian Energy Policy and Programs (OIE). These audits aimed to identity cost-effective energy efficiency measures for four essential, multi-use buildings: the Tribal Office, the Community Center, the Duplex, and the Association of Village Council Presidents (AVCP) Office. Energy-efficient retrofits would include measures such as air-sealing, installation of setback thermostats, and LED lighting upgrades. NVA has been steadily implementing energy efficiency measures based on previous audits of tribal buildings from 2017, with a primary objective of stabilizing and reducing energy costs. Understanding how a building performs regarding energy usage and cost is a key first step in determining efficiency improvement strategies. Tracking historic consumption and cost in relation to actual weather data allows a building owner to monitor changes in the facility’s performance or energy use. This data-driven approach helps to identify trends over time and pinpoint specific areas where energy consumption may be improved. NVA obtained energy audits for five buildings in 2017; this project was intended to implement high- payback recommendations such as replacing lighting with LEDs, installing programmable thermostats with setbacks, and air-tightening building envelopes. NVA and NREL expected to see reductions in building energy costs ranging from approximately 13 to 18%. These retrofits were intended to build on NVA’s long-term vision to support cost-effective building operations through energy efficiency and address goals outlined in the Aniak Traditional Council’s Energy Action Plan (Simeon et al. 2019). NVA anticipated that the outcomes from this project (regarding high-payback, simple retrofits found in the energy audit process) could be replicated with similar buildings in the village and region to avoid the time-delays and cost impacts from contracting energy audits. Other expected outcomes included increased community resiliency and reduced dependence on fuel oil shipments. The primary actors on the project were the NVA, NREL, Energy Audits of Alaska, and the Cold Climate Housing Research Center (CCHRC). As project lead, NVA made decisions on which building to prioritize, hosted vendors, and presented at OIE program reviews. NREL provided general project management, coordinated with the energy auditor to develop and administer RFPs, and coordinated travel for vendors flying to the village during implementation. NREL also gathered, analyzed, and reported project data, and assisted with quarterly progress and financial reporting.
